analysis.one_liner: Bans airlines from charging fees that exceed their actual costs for changes, bags, and seats.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on February 1, 2023 and stayed there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Department of Transportation to write rules banning airlines from charging fees that are out of line with what the fee actually costs the airline. It covers change and cancellation fees, checked and carry-on bag fees, and seat-selection fees. It also requires that parents be seated next to their children age 13 or younger at no extra charge. The bill died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers, especially budget travelers who pay bag fees, seat fees, and change fees. Families with young children would be guaranteed free adjacent seating.

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the Transportation Department, within 270 days, to write rules prohibiting fees for changes, cancellations, checked bags, carry-on bags, and seat selection that are 'unreasonable or disproportional to the costs incurred' by the airline, and to set standards for judging each type of fee.

For change and cancellation fees, the standards must account for what the airline actually gains — a canceled seat can often be resold, and cancellations can be anticipated and planned for — so airlines could only charge for their real costs, such as electronic processing and related labor.
For seat fees, the bill ensures passengers traveling with children age 13 or younger can be seated next to their children at no additional charge to them or anyone else on the flight.
The Department would have to update the fee standards at least every three years, so they keep pace with airline pricing practices.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which collected billions of dollars a year in bag and seat fees, would lose revenue from fees that exceed their costs. If airlines cannot recoup the money through fees, they may shift some of it into base fares.

drawbacks.text: Setting a legal standard for 'reasonable and proportional' fees is hard: the bill gives the Transportation Department broad discretion, and airlines could challenge any rules in court, delaying relief for years.

If airlines can no longer recover costs through fees, some of that revenue would likely reappear in base ticket prices, so travelers who check no bags or never change flights could pay a share of costs they don't personally incur.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to the tens of millions of passengers who pay bag, seat, and change fees is large and immediate, while the main cost — some fee revenue migrating into base fares — is diffuse and partly borne by infrequent flyers. The bill is a straightforward consumer-protection measure; its weaknesses are procedural (rulemaking timelines and likely litigation), not substantive.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Commerce Committee on the same day, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the FAIR Fees Act on February 1, 2023 with six Democratic cosponsors and one independent.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation that same day; no further action is recorded in its history.
The Congress ended January 3, 2025, with the bill still in committee, so no vote was ever held in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines, which keep collecting fees on bags, seat selection, and changes without any cost-based limit.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, which keep charging unregulated fees

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats or the independent Sen. Sanders; no Republican cosponsored, and the committee majority never moved the bill.

industries.note: U.S. airlines collect billions of dollars a year in checked-bag, seat-selection, and change fees, much of it above the actual cost of providing the service. The bill would cap those fees at cost, directly cutting that revenue stream. Airlines opposed similar fee provisions in this Congress.

industries.industry: Travel booking platforms and ancillary-fee intermediaries
industries.note: Sites and services that earn commissions or markups on bag and seat fees would see that revenue shrink as fees are limited to costs.
